CITY COUNCIL AGENDA; JOINT MEETING WITH PLANNING COMMISSION
March 27, 2018
  2
   MEMORANDUM
  Agenda Item #:  1-4
  Meeting Date: 03/27/18

TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL

THRU:  ANTON DAHLERBRUCH, CITY MANAGER

FROM:  SHERI REPP-LOADSMAN, PLANNING AND BUILDING DIRECTOR

SUBJECT:  DISCUSSION ITEMS FOR THE JOINT MEETING OF THE CITY
  COUNCIL AND PLANNING COMMISSION

DATE:  MARCH 27, 2018

The following are discussion items for the City Council and Planning Commission meeting of
March 27, 2018.

  A. City Council policy and vision that resulted in its decision(s) on recent appeals
  of Planning Commission decision(s).
  B. Application of Neighborhood Compatibility Guidelines in reference to
  “mansionization”, trees and views, grading, basements, decks, neighborhood
  character and achieving community consensus.
  C. Review of landscaping plans for projects to determine jurisdiction preferences
  (use of conditions of approval or reliance upon Palos Verdes Homes
  Association) for regulating view impairment of private property trees.
  D. Wireless telecommunication applications in reference to effectiveness of the
  ordinance, review/application process, and goals.

For the discussion of each of these items, staff has summarized and framed the issues as
follows:

A. City Council policy and vision that resulted in its decision(s) on recent appeals
  of Planning Commission decision(s)

  There have been several recent appeals of the Planning Commission decisions to the City
  Council. Several of those appeals resulted in additional modifications to the project
  required by the City Council.

  A list of the appeals from 2015 to present is attached to the staff report as Attachment A.
  To avoid or reduce the amount appeals, the Planning Commission should have a better
  understanding of what the City Council’s policy and vision is on these types of
  applications. The City Council relies upon the Planning Commission to review projects for
  1  001
   consistency with the General Plan, Zoning Ordinance, Neighborhood Compatibility
  Guidelines and other applicable policies. The Planning Commission works diligently to
  fairly administer the City’s requirements, maintain the public trust and adhere to the vision
  and policies of the City Council.

  The relationship between the Planning Commission and the City Council is one of trust and
  mutual respect. The relationship can become strained when there is insufficient or different
  understanding of goals, objectives or priorities. There may also be concern if the City
  Council repeatedly overturns or modifies Planning Commission decisions. Periodic joint
  meetings is one of the best tools to improve communication and to recognize shared and
  divergent opinions.

  The purpose of this discussion is for the City Council to discuss its policy and vision
  for neighborhood compatibility applications in order that the Planning Commission
  makes decisions that are consistent, thus reducing the number of appeals.

B. Application of Neighborhood Compatibility Guidelines in reference to
  “mansionization”, trees and views, grading, basements, decks, neighborhood
  character and achieving community consensus.

  Mansionization / Neighborhood Character

  The concept of “mansionization” generally involves the demolition of a smaller home on a
  lot and the construction of much larger home, often to near the maximum floor area and lot
  coverage allowed. With larger homes replacing smaller homes, the character of a
  neighborhood can change. Lower Lunada Bay and Valmonte are neighborhoods that
  residents feel are susceptible to “mansionization”.

  The Planning Commission recognizes that property owners have a right to increase the size
  of their homes. There is a careful balance to consider what is allowable under the code
  while considering the impacts to surrounding properties. Thought is also given to the deed
  restrictions put in place by the PVHA which outline what was envisioned for development.

  Trees and Views

  The Planning Commission and City Council have recently reviewed projects where mature
  trees and hedges exist on the property. In some cases the mature landscape makes it
  difficult to view the silhouette to fully assess the impacts of the project from surrounding
  properties. In some instances, the Planning Commission has expressed a desire to have
  trees removed or hedges trimmed so that they could assess the impacts of the project. In
  other cases, mature vegetation may be proposed to be removed as part of the development
  project and retention may be beneficial for both neighborhood character and environmental
  reasons.

  The Palos Verdes Homes Association has jurisdiction over private trees and have expressed
  to staff that they do not wish to have mature trees cut down, especially if the project does
  not ultimately get approved. The Planning Commission has questioned to what extent they
  should ask the applicant to remove or retain trees on private property.

  2  002
 Grading

One of the Neighborhood Compatibility findings states “that the proposed development is
designed and will be developed to preserve to the greatest extent practicable the natural
features of the land, including the existing topography and landscaping.” Grading is often
used as a tool to mitigate view and massing impacts to adjacent neighbors. If a home is too
large or too high, it is often suggested that the applicant consider grading down in order to
mitigate view, massing, and/or privacy impacts to adjacent neighbors. In addition, if the
home is buried too much into the grade, it does create high retaining walls and affects the
livability of the home. Several residents have raised concern with too much grading,
especially when the amount of grading changes the character of the neighborhood. For
example, the Planning Commission reviewed a project where a tuck under garage was
proposed and the adjacent homes included a garage at grade. The neighbors to the rear of
the project voiced concerns about view impacts and the project resulted in the entire
structure being pushed further down into the grade. These tuck under style garages may
also lead to a change in the neighborhood character and increased size of the proposed
home.

Basements

There have been several recent projects with large basement or cellar spaces that as
designed, could be utilized as livable area. The zoning code requires that all spaces with a
ceiling height of 7’ or more be counted towards the allowable floor area and ceiling spaces
between 5’ to 6’-11” in height be counted towards the gross floor area, but not allowable
floor area. It is important to note that the building code does not distinguish habitable space
solely based upon the ceiling height. Areas that are 7’ or greater in ceiling height are
deemed to be habitable. However, the inclusion of mechanical ventilation could qualify
areas less than 7’ as habitable. For example, bathrooms and laundry rooms can have a
ceiling height of not less than 6’-8”. Since the ceiling height of bathrooms and laundry
rooms is not required to be a minimum of 7’, then pursuant to the zoning code this space
would not be counted as floor area and would be counted as gross floor area. Large areas
where the ceiling height is 6’-11” could easily be converted or used as habitable space
without the proper egress and light and ventilation.

The Planning Commission recently reviewed a revised project at 2448 Via Anacapa in
which the previously approved design included a 1,058 sq. ft. cellar with a ceiling height of
6’-11” and was considered as “non-habitable” space. Given that the ceiling height was less
than 7’, the entire cellar was not included as floor area. The revised project included raising
portions of the cellar to a ceiling height of 7’ to allow a media room, bathroom, and laundry
room. With the revised design, regardless of the ceiling height, the area appeared to be
designed as habitable space and additional questions were raised as to whether or not egress
(i.e. window well) and light and ventilation typically required for habitable space should be
required. During the Planning Commission hearings, it was also discussed that if these
areas were originally proposed under grade, there could have been more relief to the more
impactful areas on the upper levels. Ultimately, the Planning Commission approved the
laundry room and window well, relocation of the wine room, and denied the bathroom.

Decks

  3  003
 The Planning Commission has recently reviewed several projects involving large second
story decks. In one instance, the proposed deck extension was opposed by both side
neighbors citing privacy and noise impacts. In another instance, the proposed deck
wrapped around the side of the residence and could pose privacy and noise impacts to the
adjacent side neighbor, however, there was no opposition by the surrounding neighbors.
Generally, large second story decks are given more scrutiny if the area can be utilized as a
congregation area and be utilized as a “party deck.” The Planning Commission has recently
expressed concerns with neighborhood character and setting precedence for large second
story decks. The Planning Commission expressed seeking clear direction by the City
Council on second story decks.

Community Consensus

With the neighborhood compatibility process, it often does not generate a community
consensus on what is appropriate in the neighborhood. If there was a consistent approach
and clear direction on how to evaluate each of the topics above, instead of evaluating the
project on a case-by-case basis, it would be possible for the applicant and the public to
anticipate what the Planning Commission and City Council is looking for and could
potentially reduce the number of hearings and appeals.

Several of the topics outlined above, have been discussed at previous joint meetings with
the City Council, Planning Commission, and Palos Verdes Homes Association. Excerpts of
those staff reports and action items are included with the staff report as Attachment B.

At the last joint meeting, the following items were discussed:

1. Status and deliverables from the City/Palos Verdes Homes Association Ad Hoc
  Committee regarding:
  a. Residential Development Process Flow
  b.  Impact Assessment Tool for Planning Commission Review
  c. Database of Residential Project Approvals (e.g. Ridge Heights,
  Garage Size, Size of Each Floor, etc.).

2. Consideration of ordinance amendment requiring certification of compliance with
  applicable declarations of covenants, conditions and restrictions (CC&Rs) Associated
  with the Palos Verdes Homes Association. The City Council directed that an
  ordinance be prepared to require private development projects to obtain PVHA
  approval prior to the issuance of any permits. The draft ordinance will be
  reviewed by the Planning Commission in April.

3. Objectives for Zoning Code Update for Accessory Dwelling Units to be in
  Conformance with New State Requirements. The draft ordinance will be reviewed by
  the Planning Commission in April.

The purpose of this discussion is for the City Council and Planning Commission to
discuss how to apply the Neighborhood Compatibility Guidelines to each of these
topics.

  4  004
 C. Review of landscaping plans for projects to determine jurisdiction preferences (use of
  conditions of approval or reliance upon Palos Verdes Homes Association) for
  regulating view impairment of private property trees.

  The Commission has discussed when it is appropriate to either condition trees to be
  removed or require hedging and landscaping to be maintained at a certain height. Staff has
  expressed that if the project is conditioned to having landscaping maintained at a certain
  height, it does become difficult for staff to consistently enforce given the limited staff and
  resources. Past direction from the City Council has also determined that the PVHA has the
  authority and process for addressing view issues associated with private landscapes.

  The purpose of this discussion is for the City Council to discuss and provide its
  direction to the Planning Commission for incorporating landscape plans as a
  condition of approval.

D. Wireless telecommunication applications in reference to effectiveness of the ordinance,
  review/application process, and goals.

  The Planning Commission and City Council have gained experience over the past several
  years reviewing wireless telecommunication facility applications. The focus has been on
  identifying the least intrusive means for the design and siting of proposed facilities. There
  has also been interest in determining if a significant gap in coverage establishes the need for
  a carrier to provide a new facility within a given area. There are increasing interests to
  provide for a more robust system that meets the need of the community for wireless
  services. At the same time, there is an ongoing interest to ensure that the neighborhood
  character and aesthetic values are protected. The City has been effective in obtaining new
  and modified facilities that have generally been viewed as successful. Now that more
  wireless telecommunication facilities are being established and a Technology Committee is
  being established, it is appropriate to reflect on the effectiveness of the ordinance, the
  process for evaluating applications, and whether the Technology Committee should become
  the board that reviews telecommunication facility applications in the future.

Notification:
The agenda for this meeting has been posted in the customary locations and in compliance with
the Municipal Code. A copy of this report has been forwarded to each Planning Commissioner
and City Council member.

  007
   Attachment B

  Basements - 10/30/12 Joint Meeting
Discussion Basement areas that are less than 7 ft. in height and the potential for future
  development.

  The Planning Commission very recently reviewed an application for new
  basement area in a home that was originally approved in 2003. During that first
  Neighborhood Compatibility process, the floor area and gross floor areas were
  carefully studied and reduced. Nine years later, the applicants came back
  requesting that the previous underfloor spaces under 7 ft. in height, be converted
  to new livable areas. There is the potential that these spaces could have been
  utilized as floor area to provide relief to the more impactful areas on the upper
  levels. Furthermore, the house could have potentially moved lower by infilling
  those underfloor spaces. In cases where there is significant underfloor area
  beneath a very large proposal, the Planning Commission would like direction
  regarding their review of this space and how to address.

Action  • The Planning Commission is to continue to be conservative with the initial
  Neighborhood Compatibility review, ensuring that the massing and size is
  appropriate for the specific neighborhood regardless of underfloor spaces.
  • Grading quantities are to be carefully examined during the Planning
  Commission process.
  • The Planning Commission has the authority to craft a condition of approval
  stating a maximum gross floor area for a project. This does not prohibit an
  applicant from resubmitting for expansion at a later date, but it does in effect
  require that future growth be reviewed by the Planning Commission again.
  • When reviewing revised applications, the Planning Commission is to be
  sensitive to previous determinations while also being aware of the
  neighborhood movement in relationship to size.

  Roof Decks - 12/2/14 Joint Meeting
Discussion Roof top decks may become more popular as property owners seek options for
  improving views. Two applications were approved within the last five months,
  one by the Planning Commission and one administratively. A third application
  has also been submitted for an upcoming Planning Commission review. Both of
  the previously approved projects were located within the Coastal Zone and the
  decks were proposed above one-story residences. In both cases, the decks were
  processed in the same manner as a second story balcony and were, therefore, part
  of the Neighborhood Compatibility review process. Neighbors provided input
  regarding view and privacy impacts and in both cases, the decks were found to be
  sensitively designed.

  There is the potential that roof top decks will become a long term trend. While
  the decks and related railing may be tucked within the surrounding roof design,
  the true impact of a group of people socializing on top of one’s roof has not been
  clearly assessed. The decks may pose greater privacy, noise, and view impacts

  008
   than originally considered. Moreover, the Code is silent regarding the potential
  for roof decks on top of a second floor, essentially creating a third level viewing
  area.

Action  Roof decks may create unforeseen privacy and view impacts, therefore,
  applications should be reviewed by the Planning Commission.

  Landscape Restriction Conditions - 11/3/05 Joint Meeting
Discussion Not available
Action  The Homes Association has made significant strides in addressing views which
  are blocked by landscaping on private property. This is being done through the
  review of new landscaping and the trimming of existing vegetation. The City
  should not begin a similar process.

  Removal of Major Private Trees - 1/30/08 Joint Meeting
Discussion Existing trees can greatly modify the impact of a project. A site may currently
  have a plethora of trees that can mitigate the visual impact of the new much
  larger home. However, it is not uncommon for existing trees to be removed in the
  course of construction due to location or damage. Because these trees can
  decrease various impacts of a project, it may be wise to require that certain trees
  remain and be actively protected during construction. Furthermore, if the tree is
  removed, a tree of comparable size and location could be required. From a
  functional standpoint, it may be appropriate to require trees over a certain trunk
  diameter to be shown on future submittals, including their disposition after
  construction, and that a standard condition be developed to protect/replace the
  trees that are shown to remain.

Action  Staff is to continue to require that all existing and proposed trees be noted clearly
  on the plans.

  Impact of Basements on Grading - 1/30/08 Joint Meeting
Discussion More architects are increasing the grading quantities to design basements and
  garages below the main level. The rationale for the increase in grading is that the
  project gets the benefit of the additional square footage while neighboring views
  are maintained. The overall massing and impact of the new structure is also
  decreased with this design. Unfortunately, while some impacts of the proposal
  are addressed, the increase in grading is a concern. The adjacent yard areas are
  sometimes excavated to meet the new lower level. Window wells are also created
  to meet light and ventilation requirements per the California Building Code.
Action  Grading for a basement is considered approvable for the sake of reduction in
  height, massing, and visual impact. However, the impact to the natural contours
  around the building is to be considered. The natural contours outside of the
  proposed structure are to be respected to the greatest extent practicable.

  009
